title: Targeting the Gender Placement Gap: Marks Versus Money
summary_en: Turkey's centralised university entrance exam shows a persistent gender gap in placement: women place less well than their scores predict. Akyol, Krishna and co-authors estimate students' preferences using a structural model and find that the gap is driven mostly by women's preferences, not by lower scores. They then compare two policy fixes: stipend subsidies for women vs. score bonuses. Score subsidies hit men with similar scores and help higher-income women, while stipend subsidies help women at little cost to men and channel benefits to lower-income women.
data_used: Administrative data from the Turkish nationwide university entrance and placement system, including students' exam scores, ranked preference lists, and final placements; structural estimation of preferences over programmes and subsequent counterfactual policy simulations.
policy_relevance: Directly relevant to Hungarian higher-education admissions (felvi.hu, ITM tertiary admissions reform): suggests that closing gender gaps in programme-level placement is better tackled through stipend subsidies than through score bonuses, because the stipend route does not displace male students at the margin and reaches lower-income women. Also a useful template for any future Hungarian audit of gendered placement outcomes in centralised allocation systems.
